title: Effectiveness of Remote Training of Long-Term Consequences of Post-COVID Cognitive Dysfunction Depending on Patient Age
abstract: The study evaluated the effectiveness of a 7-day remote cognitive training program delivered via the "Aita" mobile application in 110 patients with long-term consequences of post-COVID cognitive dysfunction. To assess the modifying role of age, the sample was stratified into two groups: Group 1 (n = 28, median age 39 years, mean time since COVID-19 3.9 ± 0.9 years) and Group 2 (n = 82, median age 22 years, time since COVID-19 4.4 ± 0.8 years). At baseline assessment, significant intergroup differences were identified: participants in the older age group demonstrated more pronounced deficits in the domains of neurodynamics, spatial memory, visual recognition, and information selection (p < 0.05). Following the one-week training program, significant positive changes were observed in both groups. In Group 1, improvements were focused in nature (neurodynamics, working memory, speed of Schulte table completion, and duplicate word search), whereas in Group 2, the restorative effect was more differentiated and encompassed all modules, including visuospatial memory and attention switching. Subjectively, participants reported moderate improvements in attention and memory and a reduction of "brain fog" (overall effectiveness: 0.48 ± 0.3 points; satisfaction: 3.63/5). Correlation analysis revealed associations between objective performance metrics and retrospective self-ratings, indicating a "regression to the mean" phenomenon and underscoring the importance of balancing cognitive load with user comfort. The findings suggest that the effectiveness of digital rehabilitation for post-COVID cognitive dysfunction is determined not by the linear time elapsed since infection, but by age-related characteristics and baseline cognitive reserve. The "Aita" application demonstrated sustained therapeutic potential; however, target domains of correction vary substantially depending on age profile, supporting the need to implement personalized, age-adapted protocols in remote neurorehabilitation practice.
